Quite good in most respects, very much like Commandos II but with more up to date graphics (even for an isometric game that's important). Mechanics are quite intuitive, moving the map with wasd+qe and the characters in point and click fashion. The characters are mostly well balanced, each with a rudimentary skilling chart which allows for you to set an emphasis on certain skills early on. Another fun thing is taking care of background tasks like foraging for food and other supplies in between missions which is something you don't find often in this kind of games but adds to the realism. To me the only sorely missing option is a non-kill one to dispose of enemies in a non-lethal way. But well, I guess WWII wasn't won on commisering the German combattants or so.

The gameplay, the setting of the game and the characters are awesome. The game is, however, filled with a lot of bugs - to the point that it's practically impossible to play on the "Hard" setting (without saving, etc).

I had a lot of fun and got my <2 EUR worth out of it, so I am still recommending it if you like this type of games.

Stealth and squad coordination feel great, the missions get genuinely challenging, and the tactical pause saves you from public embarrassment. Not revolutionary, but if you like real-time tactics and suffering strategically, it absolutely delivers.

Suddenly, you realize that a single failure means the enemies know exactly where all your group is hiding that you had just been carefully navigating them to, and you realize it is then literally and absolutely impossible for you again to enjoy the feeling of sneaking around meaning anygthing at all. And the game becaomes absolutely useless.
I cannot get a refund. Please don't pay more than two dollars for this game. It will suddenly go from seeming like you have some already sketchy but fun stealth micro-movement control to instantly you realizing the very limited scope of just click a guy around and do the exact same thing once another guard walks by. It's tedious, has no different feel between any options you might try, and the has this implied idea that you have any reason to think about resources or skill trees but they literally don't do a single thnng you can detect as useful progression.
You will, without a single doubt, suddenly realize the game will never have any of your imagined different ways to do things, and it will be ruined. You will have no interest in just clicking the guys around in teh axact same manner again but just avoiding the new timing of guards walking around like its an arcade game from the 90s. this guy walk left and right, this guy walks up and down, time it just right or suddenly your guys you snuck into the bushes far away  and out of sight will die intantly when the other guard sees your other guy and the entire base, always, all at once jiust kills whatever is near them, regardless of what you thought it menat to be hidden. One guy gets spotted,and it suddenly feels like Pac-Man when they turn blue, ALL the guards accross the map turn red at once and start running right at your hidden guys. It's truly just horribly stupid when you suddenly realize that your previous three misisions were a complete waste of time assuming you were actually being stealthy.

It's a shame, I really wanted to like this game for what it pretends to be, then the ontrols were already sketchy, but I went with it more just because I REALLY did want it to be fun trying different tactics and exploring builds, load out, loot etc ... but like  a ton of bricks, in one instant, I realized there is zero nuance or control of you options beyond, click the guy here then there and when the gaurd passes click him over there. $30??? this game is a beta that no one added anything fun to after they got clicking the guys around done.. Such a shame.

Underwhelming. The first few levels set up a game that never ends up coming together. 

The campaign has a decent beginning but they give up any semblance of an actual plot after the halfway point. All the characters are one note and get zero development throughout the game. 

The campaign itself is also longer than the core gameplay can really support. After the first 2-3 missions you'll see pretty much all the depth there is in the game, and you can really tell that they were running out of ideas in some of the later missions. The characters you unlock really only have 1 or 2 meaningful abilities that separates them from the rest and for many of them it's actually just a worst version of what another character has. This really hurts the game when the only real meaningful change to your gameplay comes from unlocking new characters through the campaign.

The game also has quality control issues. I never had a bug that hard killed my campaign, but I had a lot of minor graphic, pathing and UI glitches that forced a reload.

Ultimately I think this is a pretty subpar tactics game. The setting is the only thing that really sets it apart, but they don't really do anything with the story to make good use of that setting so I can't really even really recommend it to fans of WW2 games.

This is a really good and a unique game. Tactical games like this (like Commandos) usually doesn't have a character progression and have restrictions on which character you can pick up to your next mission.

The game also have some unique mechanics like taking cover and automatically shooting the enemies that comes in range. Shooting doesn't alert the whole map like Commandos which I continuously beaten using stealth. With Partisans, you are not afraid of shooting. In fact, you look forward to position your troops at the right location with the right cover to bring hell to your enemies.

Having said that, the game is a little bit rough around some parts. There is not enough information about some of the items you find. I am into the 10th hour and I still don't know what some items do. Some times when I just pick certain abilities, the enemies get alerted without me even using it. It's not a deal breaker but as usual with these types of games, you have to save frequently.

Last thing, I don't know Russian and the whole dialogues are in Russian which makes me a little bit disconnected. I am a bilingual person and English isn't my first language. Honestly it's bold to take a decision like that in modern gaming. I'd have appreciated it if I had the ability to listen to the dialogue in English.

If you enjoy this types of games, you will enjoy everything unique about Partisans 1941.

This game can't make up it's mind if it wants to be a Stealth game or a Tactical game, and in this case those elements are pretty exclusive and conflict with one another. I love the fact that it feels like a small resistance group in that you have to build up your camp and be wise with ammo and supplies because you can only obtain and carry so much.

I hate the fact that stealth is forced on you rather than being treated as an acceptable strategy to conserve supplies and ammo. Half the time the missions will begin with stealth that forces you to try and figure out the precise and convoluted ass way you by which you have to reach your objective, only for it to turn into a shoot-out anyway once you get there. It feels more like an extremely tedious puzzle game, and it's not fun.

The class levels are pretty bare bones and don't really offer enough, especially in the way of variety. If the game hadn't been so dead set on shoe-horning in Commandos style stealth mechanics, they probably could have done a lot more on the tactical side and really fleshed out more companions, squad structure, gear, and class levels. Instead what we got was just a woefully average game that barely makes the bar. If you're patient, it's not a bad game, if you want something more action oriented then you're better off going elsewhere.

If they ever open up a modding workshop, I can see a lot of these problems getting sorted and fixed, but I think the game has lost all its thunder by now.

The atmosphere of the game is impressive, and the ability to approach missions in different ways really enhances the feeling of guerrilla warfare. I like the classic specialization of the different heroes and the way they can be upgraded. The camp management mechanic is also an interesting idea.

On the other hand, the experience is weakened by technical flaws, such as dump AI that doesn’t notice missing comrades or even an explosion right next to it. The repetitive camp management also tends to slow the gameplay down rather than enrich it.

Still, these shortcomings can be overlooked, because in the end the game’s strengths outweigh them.

A more combat-oriented stealth strategy game with cover, freely deployed traps, and chances-to-hit based on each character's level of mastery of certain firearms. If setting up ambushes is not your thing, the game can be played slowly and more-or-less stealthily, attracting enemies one by one with lures and whistling to knife them - and this seems necessary for some achievements - but it is more frustrating that way, in part due to bugs and controls. I experienced quite a few issues with traversal, picking items off the ground, items vanishing from inventory if sorting too quickly, several crashes, and general lack of responsiveness when controlling characters, which hinders swift playing. Literally every action is performed with a simple left click, which becomes problematic when there are multiple interactive objects too close together.

Remember to always perform melee attacks on enemies from behind or from the sides, as they waste almost no time going into "red" alerted state when confronted up close, thus probably ruining the achievement run and instantly failing the occasional "do not be discovered" mission requirement, even if that enemy is neutralised shortly afterwards. At a distance on Normal difficulty setting, enemies' detection times are pretty forgiving, though. Some enemies turn their heads, and officers have a much wider field of view. Annoyingly, windows are treated as perfectly transparent openings at "ground level" and do not hinder enemy vision at all - bodies and characters in a room will get spotted by enemies patrolling outside through a window, even at a considerable distance (though this is mostly only a problem for challenge missions with all modifiers on).  The only way to hide a character by the window reliably is to click to take cover by the window sill. In addition, accidents will always attract nearby and sometimes even pretty remotely positioned enemies, and cause them to go into "yellow" search mode.

Each operative gains experience to level up and improve abilities. The descriptions on some of them could be a better, and there does not seem to be a way to reset allocated skill points. Some abilities seem more useful than others, so save in advance to experiment freely.

There is loot to be found in the levels and stashed in the operatives' inventories, even if said loot is pretty scarce in the name of balance. Some of it has to be taken back to base where it gets converted into food and "supplies", while some of it can be used in combat - stuff like weapons, ammunition, mines, grenades, lures, and healing items. There are no silenced weapons, but gun shots have limited noise range. There also don't seem to be any heavy weapons. Keep in mind, that loot cannot be placed on the ground or in containers for sorting purposes, only discarded.

Managing the base of operations is a cool concept, but it feels somewhat undercooked. It may eventually start feeling a little tedious having to assign tasks to each squad mate - things like procuring food or supplies, and performing passive "missions" with a chance-to-resolve. On the other hand, if you end up feeling some emotional attachment towards the characters, even such basic management along with equipment sorting can add to immersion. Problem is, the characters get very limited exposure because there isn't really any dramatic story here - the campaign feels more like a pack of independent missions and ends pretty abruptly.

The game features an entirely optional Hard mode which disables manual saving, and Missions mode which allows for replaying five levels with modifiers enabled to increase difficulty (only the latter mode has achievements for playing it). Get comfortable with level layouts and game mechanics first because the reinforcements modifier seems pretty savage -  it spawns squads of enemies after certain time intervals, and they just bee-line to engage player characters. Still, it can be fun to run away from them through pre-mined narrow passages.

All in all, it is good when it works, but it really needed more time in development - if for nothing else than to work a bit more consistently.

After searching for another top down stealth game similar to 63 Days or War Mongrels, I finally decided on this when I found a $4 sale.  It was definitely worth it for the game play.  It's not perfect, but so few of this type of game are perfect.  It is entertaining and engaging for the most part, and sometimes frustrating.  The 'base building' and intermission parts with the stories are almost pointless aside from letting you level up XP and get a few more gadgets.  About halfway through, I was just skipping that because I wanted to get into the levels.  If you find this at a price that's agreeable to you, I think you'll generally enjoy it.

Partisans 1941 had potential, but it’s a frustrating experience overall.

Achievements are misleading: On Steam, DLC achievements (from Back Into Battle) are mixed right into the base game list. This makes it look like you can unlock things like Missions Mode and Defense Mode, when in reality they’re locked behind paid DLC. If you only own the base game, you’ll never be able to 100% the achievements. It feels unfair and misleading for completionists.

Unresponsive UI: The interface often doesn’t respond properly. Menus lag, commands fail to register, and inventory management is clunky. In a tactics game, where precision and timing are critical, this is unacceptable.

Story & execution fall flat: Compared to Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, which delivered a far better story, polished UI, and flawless execution, Partisans 1941 feels like a rough imitation rather than a true competitor.

Unless you’re willing to buy extra DLC and tolerate buggy systems, I can’t recommend this game. If you want a polished, challenging, and satisfying tactics experience, play Shadow Tactics instead.

Partisans 1941 is a tactical stealth strategy game developed by Alter Games and published by Daedalic Entertainment, set against the brutal backdrop of World War II’s Eastern Front. Unlike many titles that focus on large-scale battles or famous military figures, Partisans 1941 zooms in on the gritty, clandestine operations of Soviet partisans fighting against the Nazi occupation. This focus on small-scale, guerrilla warfare and stealth tactics creates a unique and immersive experience, blending elements of real-time strategy, squad management, and resource gathering into a tense and challenging survival narrative.

The game’s story centers around a group of partisans struggling to survive behind enemy lines after a devastating defeat in 1941. You lead a small, ragtag team that grows over time as you rescue civilians, recruit fighters, and build a makeshift resistance base. The narrative unfolds through character interactions, mission briefings, and environmental storytelling, painting a somber and personal picture of war’s human cost. While the storyline itself is somewhat straightforward, the emotional weight comes from the survival struggle and tough decisions you have to make, rather than plot twists or grandiose drama.

Gameplay in Partisans 1941 is defined by tactical stealth and careful planning. Missions often take place in dense forests, villages, and enemy encampments where loud gunfights are a last resort. The game rewards patience and creative problem-solving—silencing enemies quietly, setting traps, and using distractions are key strategies to avoid overwhelming odds. Each mission is essentially a puzzle, where awareness of terrain, line of sight, and enemy patrol patterns can make the difference between success and annihilation. The AI is generally competent, forcing players to think several steps ahead rather than relying on brute force.

Squad management is a core pillar of the experience. You control a team of diverse characters, each with unique skills, strengths, and personalities. As you progress, you can assign roles like scout, sniper, or demolitions expert, and tailor your team’s loadout with weapons and equipment scavenged or crafted from resources. The characters develop over time, gaining experience and new abilities, which adds a light RPG element that increases investment in their survival. However, permadeath is a constant threat—losing a veteran member can be a significant blow, adding emotional stakes to every encounter.

The base-building aspect offers a strategic layer that complements the tactical missions. Your home camp serves as the hub where you manage resources, craft items, and upgrade facilities. Scavenging for food, ammunition, and medicine is essential, and managing limited supplies forces you to prioritize certain upgrades or risk the health and morale of your fighters. The base also acts as a narrative anchor, showing the gradual growth of your resistance and offering moments of respite between missions. This balance between intense combat operations and quiet base management helps pace the game well.

Visually, Partisans 1941 employs a muted color palette and detailed environments that capture the grim reality of Eastern Europe during the war. The isometric perspective allows for clear tactical views of maps, with plenty of environmental detail that supports stealth tactics—bushes for hiding, buildings for cover, and terrain features that affect visibility and movement. While the graphics are not groundbreaking, they are effective and serve the gameplay purpose well. Animations are fluid, and the sound design further enhances immersion, with ambient noises of wildlife and distant gunfire contrasting sharply with the tense silence of stealth operations.

The soundtrack is subtle but effective, blending atmospheric music with the sounds of nature and war to create an immersive auditory experience. Voice acting is competent, with dialogue that adds personality to characters without feeling overdone. The game also includes text logs and mission reports that enrich the worldbuilding, providing historical context and personal stories that deepen player engagement.

Despite its strengths, Partisans 1941 is not without flaws. Some players may find the pacing slow, especially early on when resources and personnel are limited, making missions feel punishingly difficult. The AI, while generally smart, occasionally exhibits pathfinding issues or inconsistent enemy awareness, which can lead to frustrating moments. Additionally, the game’s learning curve can be steep, particularly for players unfamiliar with tactical stealth games, as success often requires trial, error, and careful micromanagement. The UI is functional but occasionally cluttered, and some mechanics could benefit from clearer tutorials or in-game guidance.

In summary, Partisans 1941 offers a thoughtful and immersive take on World War II tactics, focusing on the gritty reality of guerrilla warfare rather than grand battles. Its blend of stealth, squad management, and base-building creates a compelling survival experience that challenges players to think strategically and value every life in their small band of resistance fighters. While it may not appeal to those seeking fast-paced action or historical epics, it shines as a tactical gem for players who appreciate methodical gameplay and a sobering portrayal of wartime resilience. For fans of strategy games with a focus on stealth and story-driven survival, Partisans 1941 is a worthy and rewarding journey into the shadows of history.

Very enjoyable, if rough around the edges. It's Commandos but Soviet, which is pretty unique. Stealth is tough but fair, and combat is short and brutal. One thing I really enjoyed is setting up ambushes: usually in tactical stealth games, gunfire is an absolute last resort or exclusively for when you're already detected. In this game, it's part of the strategy to start a gunfight on your own terms; set up crossfires, take up cover positions, put down mines. If done well, you can take down a group of fascists within a few shots without the rest being any the wiser, and pulling that off without injures on your side is satisfying.

Some things are definitely janky -- especially the UI would benefit from getting another pass, and I confess to peeking at a guide to get some basic tips to get me started because the tutorials leave much to be desired. The story is thin and strangely a-political, which seems a waste of an opportunity to show a seldom-seen perspective on the war. Party members are decently written but the enemies are all cartoonishly evil nazis, which is to say it's all pretty shallow. 

Cool game nonetheless, I'd recommend it for fans of XCOM and I'd be interested in a sequel.

A rifle may requires ammo from pistol etc.

There are a lot of squad members but you can send at most 4 characters to the battlefield or even 3 most of the time. Even the last episod, I can only send 3 members. The story also ended suddenly.

If Shadow Tactics is 8/10, this one will be 6.5/10 as the story is not attractive & the gameplay is not really enjoyable.

The amount of propaganda is... A bit too much, to be honest. 
But if you can look past that, possibly by imagining or pretending that this is a purely fictional scenario where there's a clear difference between the 'good' guys and the 'bad' guys (in a war, there never is), then this game, as a game, is pretty good.

The pros:
+Decent writing for a story-driven game, pretty engaging if you're into war themes, and the dialogues between characters are fun

[h1]Intriguing ideas, but fumbles too often to be truly great.[/h1]

Partisans is a strange game, it has some very unique features but the actual product still leaves a lot to be desired.

Unlike similar isometric stealth games Partisans has a loot system where you can pick up equipment, weapons, and ammo for use on the field. This includes food and materials which are used for the base management side of the game. It's a neat idea and your party members can make use of literally anything at their disposal no matter who they are. Need someone with rocks to throw as distractions? sure. Want a dedicated medic? easy. Party members have a couple of individual skills to differentiate them, so team member choice is important but it doesn't gate-keep specific strategies.

Another feature is the camp management between missions. You have to produce enough food to keep your team healthy, enough materials to help make improvements like weapon upgrade benches, better food production, creating items, etc. So long as you assign everyone a job around production and food each day and upgrade as soon as possible it quickly becomes a non-issue and sadly kind of redundant, which is a shame since as a concept it's pretty solid.

That's also kind of where the good points end...

The first and biggest problem with this game: it has fog of war. From a planning perspective this is a terrible idea for real-time stealth when timing and line of sight is paramount. Enemies can even sometimes see you but are covered by the fog so you end up being spotted by someone you didn't even know existed. This really slows down some levels where you're consigned to moving to a crawl inching forward hoping no one is in the distance. There isn't a dedicated crouch or prone action and instead you have "stealth mode" where you move slower and crouch once you get close enough to an enemy. Their FOV cone is their full absolute vision...sometimes anyway, not often with how buggy this mechanic is.

The next problem is the controls. Left click as a command literally does [b]everything[/b]. Movement, picking up bodies, interacting with objects, the lot. When areas get cluttered you quickly end up doing the wrong action since something else was either close by or in the way. Having ctrl + click would prevent this but you can't remap any controls at all. The pointer precision is also off so you can't be exact with your movements or actions so sloppy looking mistakes are genuinely through no fault of your own.

Another dealbreaker is the map scrolling with the mouse bugs out constantly. Fighting the camera and having to correct it with the arrows keys was painful and shouldn't still be an issue after the game has been out for so long.

AI detection is probably the biggest offender though because it doesn't even play by its own rules. In every other game of this kind when you're seen the enemy's view cone becomes focused so you know who it is, but here you get nothing but a small exclamation mark above the enemy's head, and if they're in fog of war? nothing. The detection gauge also fills based on noise. Fine in theory, but the noise detection radii doesn't match the noise radii you make as yours is apparently way bigger than what it says. Enemies will still hear you even if you think you're out far enough away. Even moving slowly into bushes can set it off so everything you think is safe carries some weird disproportionate risk. There's no delay between being spotted and the alarm being sounded so multi-kills can be unnecessarily hard to execute properly.

Sometimes an enemy can instant alert the second you hit their FOV with no detection gauge fill - I can't work out if it's something to do with being spotted beforehand or if it's a bug? Being in vision whilst carrying a body is also an instant alert, made worse with carrying bodies being incredibly slow even with party members who can upgrade that stat. I've sometimes even had enemies who are off my screen the other end of the map being "alerted" to my presence?

The next issue is the "tactical mode". For some reason you have to execute the plan the second you leave the mode, which can be awkward if you want to scout before confirming your actions. It's a small quality of life difference but a big thing when compared to other games that use the same system. With the tiny detection alert window on top I mostly gave up using this and opted for strictly using solo kills instead since they were far more reliable.

For a stealth game there's a lot of combat you're forced into. Sections of the map act as cover, and hit chances are calculated based on range, weapon stats, and enemy cover much like an XCOM-esque title. If in cover you can normally let the fights play out themselves and you'll come out mostly unharmed. Overall though I'm not entirely sold on this concept since more often than not these fights are against an army of 12+ enemies vs your 3 team members, and slow methodical stealth mechanics here are clumsy enough. If there were smaller groups to deal with and not have the whole map be alerted when you fight then maybe this could work, but definitely not in its current state.

The map design is your standard fare of large forests, train stations, enemy bases, however there's no verticality so no ladders or vantage points to make use of. These maps are also massive but also where the designs have problems. 90% of the time you can skirt around the perimeter of a map and avoid a lot of troublesome stuff. [spoiler]The last mission becomes trivialised by doing this as you can just sneak to the top corner, fetch the key needed and you're into the main building with zero effort. After that, I opted to just run and gun my way through to the final room because apparently there's one type of enemy that refused to walk through open doorways so I could spam grenades through until they were all dealt with.[/spoiler]

In summary, Partisans has a novel approach to real-time stealth with a unique blend of RTS, top-down shooter, and resource management but is severely bogged down by a very finicky system, odd bugs, and mechanics that just don't really mesh well together on the whole. There's some interesting foundation being built here though, but it still needs a fair bit more polish to really make a dent on their competition.

I want to give this a 'maybe' or a 'neutral' rating, but I'll settle for a tentative 'yes'.

At its core, the game has a decent idea. Stealth real-time-with-near-pause, with party control. It is also point-and-click with simple mechanics. 

However, the execution leaves much to be desired. Given how it is point-and-click to execute actions, there really needs to be more feedback to the player as to how the characters will behave in certain situations. For example, if a door is locked and the player attempts to move a character into a position behind it, the character will attempt to path into the room by any means necessary. Even if this would put the character in a position where they can be seen. There is no indicator that pathfinding was not able to find the shortest direct path and is, in fact, attempting to go a longer route to get to where the player clicks.

Combat is not particularly satisfying in this game. Your characters and the enemy both go down in one or two shots, and there are far, far more of them than you. By virtue of sheer number of shot attempts, if your stealth breaks and things go loud, you are pretty much done. The enemy will overwhelm your position with sheer volume of fire, and it doesn't seem like they have limited ammunition either while you are limited.

Stealth is where this game is strongest. Each level is essentially a puzzle to be solved. Which enemies do you eliminate first? How do you choose to eliminate them? These choices can make or break each run. However, it has to be said that the optimal path is often the ONLY path you can take, because doing anything else would break stealth - and doom your run by virtue of loud firefights going very badly for your partisans.  Taking a leaf out of Sniper Elite, you can use bottles and rocks as distraction tools as well, which helps things along. 

All in all, there are frustrations with the game with regards to both the level design and the way that the  controls behave. A little bit more feedback to the player as to how the characters will move with a given input would be nice. There are bugs with detection triggering well beyond sight cones, and sometimes with enemies detecting things behind walls. But if you can overlook these, you can certainly have a pretty good time in the game.

Worth your while if you are a fan of Commandos style tactics-games. Ideally get it on sale as the technical side leaves a lot to be desired. If you can't stand communisits don't play.

PROS
- Most of the missions are wonderfully designed, great looking, with multiple ways to complete your objectives. They're not too long nor unreasonably difficult. Mission 14 is genuinely a masterpiece of non-linear stealth action.
- Soundtrack and sound overall is very good and atmospheric, good weapon sounds and nice ambience. Visuals have a nice artstyle and are overall very pleasant.
- Characters are reasonably well balanced, they all offer different flavours and unique approaches to missions. Cracks in their balancing appear only at very late game or at higher difficulties.

MIX
- Story is pretty much non-existent as there isn't an overarching plot. The characters don't go through arcs or change, although for this type of a game it isn't much of an issue. You are given missions to complete and that's it. Extra interactions between characters would've been nicer though.
- The camp managment side is very barebones, you get most of your camp upgrades very early and after that there isn't much to do. Also the camp UI is kind of messy and you never get quite used to it.
- The game feels like playing through a Yuri Ozerov movie, it very much uses USSR WW2 propaganda, the Partisans are all super heroic, the Germans are all super bad and there are one-liners straight out of propaganda posters. Now this might be on purpose to create an atmosphere reminiscent with what the state media would portray the war as, shortly after it's end (think post-war US WW2 movies). Or the developers genuinely believe this and are old-school USSR apologists. Either way be warned, it might rub some people the wrong way.

CONS
- The game doesn't have fully customisable graphics, you cannot choose textures, objects and post processing individually, you can only chose low. medium and high presets, that's it.
- The inventory is total crap, not the idea, but the implementation. The game will scream at you that you don't have anymore space but you actually do, you just have to make it manually. Items of the same type often won't autmoatically stack together, so you get three incomplete stacks of the same ammo instead of one full stack. You cannot reload your guns in the inventory by dragging ammo onto them, you have to unload the gun and then put it into the Partisans hands. Every time you move an item or change a weapon the game lags. The auto sorting is almost useless as it sorts very strangely and makes a mess. The icons are very difficult to read at first glance, you will confuse different ammo types till the very end.
- There are many moments where the game hiccups and you'll have no idea why, it's classic Slav-jank. 'Cause I'm a Slav myself I don't really mind and just use the F5 button religiously as I was taught, but it's noticeable enough to where it can be sometimes frustrating.
- The last 2 missions are exactly the opposite of why I liked the game. They are very linear, ball bustingly hard and feel like you need to cheese to finish them. Absolutely appalling ending to an otherwise good game.

(-) Bugs:
a. Partisan stuck in a object. I have to restart mission 14 because of this.
b. Input Command not registered 
c. Placed trap suddenly disappear 
d. Partisan suddenly stops when placing trap/mine 
e. Partisan suddenly stops when activate a skill 
f. Hard time to examine/loot enemy body. Have to move the body first or rotate the camera, before the “Bag” cursor properly work. 
g. Hard time to examine/loot crate/box. Have to move the mouse precisely to make the “hand” cursor appear.
h. Graphical bugs 
i. Inventory UI did not respond, can’t click or drag item 
j. Save did not properly remember enemy position. Let’s say if an enemy patrolling from point A to B and then to C. I save the game when he reaches point C. If I load the save file, he appeared randomly on his patrolling path, so if he spawn on A or B… I have to wait for him to reach point C AGAIN. 

(-) Tactical Mode
Don’t think that it’s the same with Shadow Mode in Shadow Tactics, which you can command each character to do specific things and execute them in any order anytime you want… Tactical Mode in this game is just slowing the time, when you press “space”, Partisan WILL immediately execute your command.

(-) Inventory Management
At first, It reminds me of Commandos 2 mechanic… but:
a. You can’t put unwanted items in the box/crate, so if your inventory is full and want to take another items… you have to destroy it.
b. There are too many items to manage. Foods, medical items, medical parts, materials, weapons, weapon parts, traps, etc... it feels like survival game rather than RTS game.

(-) Save restriction
You won’t be able to save in 3 conditions:
1.Hard difficulty
2.Enemy is alert (alarm is raised)
3.Your character is busy. Let’s take one example, If you’re using Sanek’s disguise ability, you won’t be able to save. You need to take off his disguise first if you want to save.

Remember that the cyberware used by the Germans in WW2 was vastly superior to everybody else's? This game has that covered. 
An enemy manages to be shocked before dying? You better believe all his friends in a radius will know what's up.
You know how when you fire a gun the sound keeps clinging to you? This game has that, making the sniper completely useless because every soldier will track her across the map with pinpoint accuracy until the first shot was fired at her no matter how many bushes houses and other things you get between you and the pusuers. After that you may be able to disengage, but let's be real, by that point you already pressed F8. Rember, the sniper is a woman and has the sprint ability, making her about double as fast as everyone else except murder chick, so you may have to wait for 20 seconds before the enemies reach you, but they still know you are there. It could also be a workaround for the stupid AI and the very limited escalation options of the maps.
You know that a body hit by a knife drops harder than a body that has just cut its throat because the knife adds weight to it? Yeah, I think the drop sound is about three times louder.
If you trigger the alarm the Germans will activate their tactical net and their heat vision and suddenly no visual cover is safe anymore. Thank god for 1941 energy restrictions, or else they would have had that stuff on the whole time.

* Every one of your soldiers has a bit of backstory and there are little talks between them that don't overstay their welcome.

Carry a lot of stuff? Outperformed by literally everybody who is not  a woman or a child. Melee? See above, except that murder chick get's to join the "equal-or-better" club. Carry heavy stuff (bodies): Also something all the grown-up males get to do. Jumping over fences? Oh, wait, that skill belongs to somebody else.

Some general flaws to an otherwise good game:
-  Side-missions and secondary objectives appear to have zero impact on the game.   There are no extra rewards or changes to the story.
- The developers managed to create a resource economy where ammunition remains scarce (very much a plus) but not weapons themselves.  At first, you covet that first common-quality MP-40.  But, by the end of the game, you may have a dozen of them and are flush with weapons and no ammo.  Yes, you can take them apart for "resources".  But I would have preferred to have *something* that could be done with those weapons.  Perhaps another mini-game of keeping other bands of partisans armed, or having a mechanical where weapons deteriorate and need to be repaired by cannibalizing surplus weapons.
-  Although there are multiple solutions to each of the levels, you'll find yourself relying on 1-2 little tricks that may get repetitive.  For example, placing a bottle to keep luring soldiers away from the group.
- The resource management is somewhat imbalanced and not finely-tuned.  You will find a combination of medical supplies, tools, clothing, etc, but these are all abstracted as "supplies".  A lantern takes twice as much space as clothing - so why take the lantern?  Splitting supplies into different types (medical, etc) could have made it more intuitive to pick which loot to bring back to the partisan base.
- I had strange bugs related to the save feature and, in a couple cases, had to restart a level from the beginning.
- Lag during inventory management in the camp.
- The overall story is a bit anti-climatic in the end.

[h1]Introduction[/h1] Partisans 1941 is an isometric stealth game and a modern successor to the Commandos series.

The game and its storyline depicts a fictional tale, taking place on the Eastern Front in WW2 as you command a group of Soviet partisans against the evil German occupiers. 

So, let us begin!

[h1]Game Review[/h1]

Partisans 1941 is an epic stealth game, with great immersive mechanics that allows the player to get lost in the gameplay (a sign of a well-made game).

You start out as a lone partisan and obtain a perfect opportunity to escape the guards. At the end of the first mission, you obtain new companions. As the game goes on, you encounter new companions, each with a limited story and you embark upon partisan activities to beat the Germans.

The stealth and strategic approach to the tactical gameplay is amongst the best I have ever played in the genre. I wholly found myself enjoying every moment of the game, as well as liking it so much, I spoke about it with friends.

However, as the game drew to its conclusion, I was found left wanting a lot more, and I felt the game ended way too soon (about 40-50 hrs for the average player). A storyline such as the one the developers were attempting to tell, I feel, could have lasted a lot longer and the gameplay was certainly capable of driving the players on to a game lasting twice as long as it did.

As I got towards the end of the game, I also encountered a game-breaking bug where one of my partisans wouldn't fire any weapon other than a pistol. This issue is almost universal amongst the playerbase, was reported to the developers many times, however, the developers ignored the complaints and did not fix the issue. This, in conjuction with the abrupt ending, left a lasting bitter taste to an otherwise perfect game experience.

[h1]Is the game worth the price?[/h1]
No, I do not think Partisans 1941 is worth its non-sale price of £24.99. In my opinion, with how many games are now released, one should always seek to acquire a game for under £10 when possible. Due to the abrupt ending and a story that was rushed to its conclusion, this game is not a must-have now, at any price. Had the game lasted 10 missions more, my opinion in regards to that may differ. Nevertheless, Partisans 1941 is a game that is often on sale on Steam or other sites for under £4. At that price, the game is a STEAL and I would recommend it to anyone who either loves, likes, or may have an interest in a tactical isometric stealth game.

[h1]What will I get from playing Partisans 1941?[/h1]
- A relaxing musical score. This game helped me overcome a really nasty illness I was struck down with.
- Engaging and really unique tactical gameplay, an isometric lovers' dream.
- A good story (but let down by its abrupt ending)
- WW2 lore (specifically Eastern Front lore)
- A game providing immense fun for 50+ hours.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Despite its flaws, Partisans 1941 is still a really good game. Alter Games, like all developers, should always fix bugs when reported by the players, and the developers lose marks for ignoring this widespread issue for several years. In addition, the abrupt, rushed ending to the story leaves a bitter taste to [i]anyone[/i] who appreciates a great story, which, as a writer of fiction, I [b]absolutely[/b] do.

The gameplay is rich, and it compliments the strategy/tactics/stealth genre extraordinarily well. 

Yet, despite its impressively immersing gameplay, at the end of playing the game, I was happy to have played it, yet I was ultimately left wanting more.

[h1] Outro [/h1]

Due to the rushed ending, as well as game-breaking bugs being ignored, I must rate this game an 8/10. Had I not encountered either issue, I absolutely would have given this game a perfect score.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Shallow combat.

I think some negative reviews make the mistake of comparing this to the Mimimi games (Desperado, Shadow Tactics), from which it copies many elements, especially the mission UI, but this game has a different playstyle and aesthetic. They will then proceed to hunt you down, always know where you are and will follow you through bushes and any obstacle you can put in between. Remember that flanking is very difficult, because they will know where the guy is that you've been hiding in a bush. The game seems to encourage you to play everything stealth which I typically enjoy (played both commandos and og men of war, but will sometimes put you into situations where combat is forced and therefore not fun.

Let's move on to both UI and object/world interaction with your characters.

I'd argue that most of the things I dislike are more personal, but there are definitely some adjustments that could be made for a better quality of life. Where I do have issues is that there are times that my characters seem to not respond properly to what I want them to do.

A decent game marred with issues. Partisans 1941 could have been the modern Commandos successor I've been waiting for, but no. It's far too unpolished and sloppily designed to earn that pedigree. I still enjoyed my time with the game, but it left me unsatisfied and just made me wanna play Commandos again.

The presentation is top notch. I'll give it credit. It's a beautiful game. I'd say it's not as vibrant as Desperados 3, but it has higher graphical fidelity. The character models are all very detailed and recognizable from afar. The game's muted color scheme adds to the bleak tone. Levels are decently sized and detailed. Voice acting is meh. The English voices are especially mediocre. There's not much to say about the soundtrack either. It's forgettable, but fitting. Performance on the other hand is spotty at best. Numerous levels dip below 60 FPS into the 30s. This is not the worst the technical issues get.

The gameplay is the highlight here. Every character has a unique ability to differentiate themselves from one another. However, they must be unlocked in a skill tree where most of the skills are the same between each character. The stealth gameplay will be familiar with anyone whose played Commandos or Desperados. You can hide bodies, pause with the space key, set traps, and die very quickly. The big difference here is that combat is an option. In a few sections, combat is inevitable and it's actually quite good. All characters' loadouts are customizable with a proper inventory system. Injuries can be sustained from combat which can affect overall accuracy or movement speed. There's a cover system as well. The way combat and stealth synergize here is great and my favorite aspect of the game. Utilizing stealth to whittle down enemy squads and setup advantageous positions for shootouts was fun. This is more than I can say for the camp management.

For a game with so many playable characters, the fact that most missions only allow up to three characters to be brought and one of them is almost always Commander Zorin is a backwards design decision. Considering you don't know the objectives, map layout, and enemy types before entering the mission, you just end up using the same squad for every mission. I never used the old man even once outside of the mission where he's rescued. Camp management is boring and repetitive. Just keep the food in the positive and you'll never lose morale. I've never seen morale go down even once. I built every optional building long before the final mission and almost never crafted anything since you can get them from missions or base operations. The only resource I needed was XP.

The story is virtually nonexisting. I can give you a general premise, but I could not recite the "plot" of Partisans. There are no memorable characters. None of them have any personality or catchy one liners. There's almost no villain. There's few cutscenes. To be honest, most of the missions were kinda forgettable. Most of them look the same since there all in some forest-y area with tons of bushes to hide in. The few instances of rainy levels and a snowy level were welcome changes of pace. I liked the prison break level as well. However, these levels have no story. They all just feel like video game levels with a brief description to give context and nothing more. The game's not even that hard. I didn't even realize I was playing the final mission when I started it and it was an awful mission. All that effort for a little speech and an abrupt fade to credits.

And then there were bugs. This game still needs patches. I'm baffled at the level of unpolish here. Characters holding their knife as if it were a rifle. Enemies spotting me and attacking through walls. Characters running in a circle in place. Enemies getting alerted from spotting hidden bodies they were nowhere near to. One of my manual saves was mysteriously deleted. The game crached once on me. UI prompts would not work as they should. Body carrying animations would glitch. Assassination animations wouldn't play as they should. Characters wouldn't shoot through open doorways, but enemies would still shoot them back. There are a lot of bugs here.

Commandos 2 was buggy as well, but it was also an extremely ambitious game with a lot of depth and imaginative design. A genuine diamond in the rough. Partisans 1941 feels like a familiar concept shoddily executed. I'm sorry, but this has nothing on the excellent design of Mimimi's brilliant trio of Shadow Tactics, Shadow Gambit, and the G.O.A.T., Desperados 3. It's a shame that the devs didn't give this game enough love to fix these issues. As it stands, it's one of the better titles in this niche sub-genre of Commandos-likes, but not one of the best. 7/10

Engaging open-fire is an interesting additional to the predominately stealth-based genre. Sometimes it's the best, and most efficient, way to tackle a problem. It's also nice to have the option. Getting spotted doesn't always mean a loaded save. However I do wish they explored this approach a bit further. There's very little to do once you're in a fire-fight. Leaving cover is risky, and slow, and you'd wished you'd set up someone on a flank before engaging (which kind of defeats the purpose of why I liked it as a stealth-alternative, if I'm utilizing stealth to establish position I might as well utilize that same stealth to kill). Additionally with a percentage-based hit-chance on enemies, missing may result in them having time to reach cover themselves, further reducing your success rate and forcing you to painstakingly re-position mid-fight (I can't stress how bad an option this is), or load a save.

As part of this open-combat system however, is the nice addition of equipment and load-outs (something you don't see from Shadow tactics/Desperados). Having different weapon choices, and multiple different utility options, is a nice touch.

Rolling with the positives; I thought the 'base section' in between missions was added value. Choosing some automated assignments/missions to gain rewards, of which you can decide is most beneficial, is a good addition.

There's some annoying tech issues regarding UI at higher resolutions/aspect ratios. My normal fixes weren't applicable either. Playing windowed was tolerable, but you don't necessarily want to play a video game to 'tolerable standards'.

Also a really bad design decision regarding saving plagued my missions. You cannot save during certain character actions. Some make sense, some do not. This however was not a gripe I ever experienced with Shadow tactics or Desperados. For example; you cannot save when one of the characters is utilizing a disguise. This is extremely painful as he moves at a significantly reduced speed while disguised, and you ultimately want to save after you've got him in a position to distract somebody (while disguised) before initiating a kill command with another character. This leads you to need to not only think about how you're going to execute a stealth-kill, but also think about where you can hide the disguised character so that you can de-disguise without being spotted, save, stay safe while waiting for disguise to come off cooldown, before going back into position. Unnecessary and a real headache considering how I felt the few missions I did in my short playtime leaned heavily on this ability.

The worst human conflict in history has arrived at the doorstep of the Soviet Union. Pacts, non-aggression agreements and an adventurous albeit misguided expedition into Finland has not prepared the USSR fully for what has showed up with a deadly blade at its throat. The Motherland has been invaded on every front. The industrial heart of the USSR, Ukraine, has been seized by the Germans and Belarus is facing endless purges of villages. The Red Army leadership, having just narrowly survived the Great Purge, is forced to retreat to the cities of Leningrad, Moscow and Stalingrad. The Third Reich holds the industry hostage, but now - they must grasp the lifeblood of the nation. The tendrils of German fascism pierce like a bayonet into the iron heart of the USSR and as the Red Army reorganizes for a desperate defense, for an eventual desperate push, they must rely on the partisans left behind.

Anyone who believes themselves too small to make a difference, have never tried to sleep in a humid room, on a summer night, with a single fly buzzing around them. The partisans are greatly outnumbered and many of them lack the ideological loyalty of the Red Army. The feared insurgents that strike the vulnerable veins and arteries of the invading German plunderer are motivated instead by a renewed civic nationalism and a loyalty to freedom from life under occupation. If one is incapable of fighting formally for their country, at the very least they can die for it.

The Second WWII/Great Patriotic War has become a biblical event in the modern world, especially for the former Soviet Bloc. To this day, its imagery, heroic tales and also the unspeakable horrors that occurred during the Eastern Front, have forever remained a stronger creation myth to the modern Russian people than the story of Adam and Eve. In much the same way how the Pacific War of the same conflict had forever changed the geography of Far Eastern Nations and created today, the major powers of the Pacific that stand now, much of Eastern Europe remembers this war with equal amounts horror, sorrow and also appreciation for a generation of men, women and even children, who endured the endurable and overcame arguably one of the greatest armies of mankind. 

But not everyone had a choice. Whether it be forced recruitment, conscription, "moral obligation" or merely survival, humanity's greatest conflict is home to some of humanity's greatest stories. Are all of them true? Unlikely, but as humans, we cherish the ideal stories just as much as we mourn the reality. 

Truly, the second world war was a behemoth meeting of superpowers and often, a lot of what lead up to it was nearly nonsensical, but almost fated by the fact that the world only tolerates one superpower at once. The war of Germany against Eastern Europe was two spheres of civilization clashing. At an immense and great cost, Stalin's communism had turned the USSR into a superpower by the end of the war and Hitler already had a mountain of corpses and destruction from the last war to build a similar beast out of the remnants of Germany.

Ignoring the political ramifications of those, today, who assert a modern revisionist soviet identity (in reality, a civic Russian nationality that ignores the significance of other nationalities of the 'near abroad') - this game is really about a nation, that was composed not just of Russians, but Kazakhs, Ukrainians of a much broader and stronger identity than merely 'communist', etc who fought off an invasion and in turn, had to become beasts themselves. The USSR is not sinless, but this game exists not to critique the USSR as much as it is to be fun.

The game is Russian jank, so there will be immense headaches. But the characters, of a variety of backgrounds and spoken languages (play this game in the Russian dub, obviously) are distinct enough to make missions a nightmare or a breeze. Personally, my preferred character selection actually made this game overwhelmingly easy, especially after I got a former prisoner with a whistle-lure and rib-shank ability. The later stages of the game became less about trial, error and patience and more about patience, as I expertly maneuvered partisans to attack in synchronized stealth ambushes.

The game allows you to go loud fairly often and whether you are fighting locals who have sold out their country to work for Germany or the elite infantry of the SS, the ability to actually pause combat and orchestrate your coordinates attacks mid firefight in a nearly RTS way, gives the game incredible leverage for when ♥♥♥♥ goes south. However, some levels are timed and have insta-fails for breaking stealth in certain sections. These are simultaneously the best and worst missions by far. The first stealth only mission was entirely garbage, but there is a part where you enter a Dulag (don't worry, the loading screens, despite last less than a second, will give you the definition of this almost every single time while playing) and it is by far some of the most fun I've had in a game of this sort in a long time.

The UI scaling is complete trash, a lot of the UI itself is hostile to the user and sorting ammo is a screaming nightmare. If you try and play too casually, your partisans will waste ammo in an engagement a literal 14 year old with a double-barrel hunting shotgun could accomplish with some coordination and the path finding is somehow worse than Warhammer 40k's first Dawn of War. Moving groups all at once rather than individually will sometimes result in an ambitious partisan, often unsuccessfully, sneaking between the gaps of standing German SS soldiers or moving around a building, sometimes through a building, in clear view of the entire German army. 

The door system is atrocious and combined with the fact the game mandates constant save scumming, you sometimes end up wasting a lot of time setting up for a simple scoop-and-poop house raid, only to be playing the RNG game of "will the German with his 360 degree Naruto side character vision see me through this wall as I stab his boyfriend", and that is IF you don't happen to open the wrong door, revealing your entire team to the German garrison like they had just won a gameshow and their prize is relentlessly murdering you instantly with submachine gun fire.

It is impossible to give a definitive answer to what makes an artistic product good, but it seems to me, tonal coherence of various components is a good starting point. This is the most important reason why I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. Right from the opening sequence Partisans 1941 is very clear in what manner it is going to depict the partisan activity, and not a single component here disagrees with the others.

When it comes to Soviet World War II Cinema the existence of two different camps is quite evident. On one hand there are war movies, such as Ballade o soldate (Ballad of a Soldier), or Jariskatsis mama (Father of a Soldier). Soviet war movies are slightly revanchist, but still hopeful of rebirth with an optimistic outlook on human psyche, even during one of the most barbaric invasions of recent history. On the other hand, there are partisan movies, such as Voskhozhdenie (The Ascent), or Idi i smotri (Come and See). There is an irremissible sombreness in partisan movies, usually depicting the barbaric actions of the Nazi war machine fully and we see that not even the Soviet people can be defined as "good".

Partisans 1941 takes partisan movies, depicts the barbarism like they do but also adds optimism and revanchism of war movies to the mix. This works very well from a narrative standpoint, considering Alter Games are on unbroken land here, with their debut game as well. It is refreshing to have hopefulness, determination, a leader that you can look up to in a work about partisans. It fills the player with a sense of appreciation towards the countless partisans operating during the most horrifying and oppressive invasion in recent history.
 
The gaming medium is perfect for this. Characters can talk about taking the war to the Nazis in any other medium, but player agency, the manner in which you will carry it out, especially with the various special skills and varied partisans this game offers is what makes it so satisfying. Having a choice between rushing a Nazi with a knife in your hand (Morozov) or picking his head from distance with a fully upgraded AVS-36 (Valya) or making him eat lead through a wall with your buckshot (Trofim) and many other options that benefit from different abilities complementing each other massively differentiates this from other media.

Even then, the first thing that grabbed my attention was not gameplay mechanics, but how good our main character (probably inspired by real life partisan commander Simcha Zorin) looked. He is clean shaven with hair like he just left the most fashionable barber shop in Byelorussia five minutes ago, with a determined look in his eyes that says I will eliminate every single Nazi from Minsk to Staroe Selo. The thousand-yard stare, the downtrodden look, the desperation from hunger and cold so associated with the partisans does not have a place here. This goes for every character. They look, talk and act like they have the hindsight to know these days will pass like any other and they will emerge victorious.

As I said, Partisans 1941 is a game where nothing is out of place tonally, and this extends even to the colour scheme. If you have played one of the numerous WWII FPS's taking place in the Eastern Front, you will already be accustomed to the yellowness of wheat, greenness of pine trees and brownness of the earth. How the game changes this well established formula is subtle, but effective. Brightness and intensity of every colour is slightly increased in comparison to usual, and a small amount of shading applied to borders of every object makes them more pronounced. These small changes give the usually depressing Soviet countryside a much more humane appearance.

As a final layer of finish, the OST is composed with the same design perspective that is present in other areas. The music you'll hear the most,[url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5JIx_-PQ5Eg] guitar track [/url] that plays whenever you're in camp is in the same vein. It's slow tempo, but the notes are crisp and distinguishable, in contrast with the melancholic vocal accompanying it, fully embracing the duality.

Of course, as both a debut game and an indie game, Partisans is far from being perfect. UI is sometimes buggy and unresponsive, especially in inventory and picking up items/bodies. It is obvious to see the game was designed with stealth options as a priority. The enemy AI can get really stupid and there will be no way to predict if they will function or not in a firefight. Camp management starts out interesting for one or two missions, but gets repetitive fast. If you have a completionist streak, you'll find that scouring every map to remove every Nazi from existence gets tiresome in larger levels, especially when they start to call in reinforcements. 

Nevertheless, when it works, it works really well. The excitement and subsequent relief of a well-executed stealth attack with combined partisans is a feeling that is rarely replicated in gaming and usually passes as a high point of a game, here these opportunities are dime a dozen. The planning it takes to silently kill a dog and its handler, usually a mid-tier enemy in most games, is rewarding thanks to the multiple approaches you can take. If you can handle some minor jank (and nothing good ever happens without some minor jank), Partisans 1941 is a game that exactly knows what it wants and achieves what it wants and this is nothing to be scoffed at in these times.

This is a good stealth title in the style of the Commandos series, set in the Soviet Union on the Eastern Front of World War II. It manages to handle such a bleak time in history with care, showing the depravity of the Nazi regime while not coming across as just an ultra nationalistic romp on the Soviet side that a lot of war films and media tend to do. You are partisans, guerrilla fighters trying to survive and push the fascist invaders out. I highly recommend using the native language with subtitles for immersion, as it's weird having Soviets with English accents and Germans well, not speaking German.

Over the course of the game you'll get around eight partisans over the course of the campaign who all have different strengths to help you on your mission. You'll be scavenging for resources and eventually have a home base of your own where you gather food, go out on reconnaissance and craft needed supplies and even upgrade your weapons. There's even a level up system and since you do get experience per kill, it can be worth it to kill as many guards and collaborators as you can, though the experience does provide diminishing returns for balance reasons. Plus in stealth games I find it usually better to get rid of as many enemies as you can to avoid yourself headaches later in a mission.

One nice thing about this game is you have the option to 'go loud' in shootouts if you end up being detected though it's highly recommended to do this towards the end of a mission once you've thinned out their ranks. You are often outnumbered and out gunned and can get injured and killed quite easily. You can slow down time to coordinate the perfect ambush. I can't describe how satisfying it is throwing grenades, setting up mines and tripwires and mowing down your enemies with surgical precision. Then slipping away like you were never there.

It's a bit buggy however and the dlc is definitely in a rougher quality than the main game. Definitely worth checking this game out as I think this game is a hidden gem. As with all stealth games, quick save and quick load are your friend. Good luck and good hunting.

They are survivors from a war nobody wanted and it's your job to weaken the enemy by taking part in different missions with a good map variety as well diferent objectives with some good optional ones as well.

The approach in each mission is really up to you. Full stealth using only your knife during an entire mission, gun-crazy with a variety of rifles, handguns and SMS or an even louder approach with grenades and mines. However the game really shines when you decide to go full stealth or at least stealth without being found (like many games, an yellow exclamation point means they know something's up, a red one means you've been found). I found out the best combo is full stealth with luring techniques. For instance you can use one character to whistle to lure a soldier and another one to use a throwing knife on him making a good combination. You can also create noises or even let a fallen body on a visible way to lure more enemies and when all of them are grouped you toss a grenade or even better a mine right next to that fallen body for maximum damage with a use of a single item.

During the game you have more tasks then simply carrying on with these missions. You don't have a base so you will have to build one. For that you will need resources so try to scavange when possible the houses, boxes and closets to find these supplies needed to build a better settlement. You keep what you got after each mission and you have a storage to keep the items so grab what you can so you can have a bigger variety of weapons for different sorts of missions.  As you progress, you will be able to improve and craft weapons as well having a place to smoke food and other surviving necessities. During early in the game I always felt I was a bit short of supplies and food but don't worry, you'll have just enough to get by another day. I believe this is intentional because when you are on the run there's not plenty of food and resources so you need to work with what you can.

Speaking of resources you can also find food during your mission but pay attention to what you loot. An icon with a red color means you are about to steal from your own people. While food is critial for your own survival, to steal from your own will decrease your morale. A low morale score will have an impact on the performance of your members. Just stick to scavaging everything you can and leave the rest for those who have even less than you. 

After all, everyone is a victim of this invasion.

After each mission you have some tasks to do in your settlement and stories to listen from your group. These make a nice change of pacing, an opportunity to slow down, calm down, get to know a bit more about each one and a chance to organize your things before going to the next mission. Rumours will also arrive at your settlement, you will read about patrols getting more frequent, soldiers now using more dogs to detect explosives and other intel that puts you inside the world in a more real form.

Day and night cicles will have an effect on your enemie's vision so use the darkness of night wisely when available and during day missions don't be afraid of trying different strategies. You can try to kill as little as possible going straight to the goal or go for a more secure but time investing path which focus on eliminating all your enemies in order to sacavanger for supplies freely. Make good use of "accidental" kills when possible. Perhaps that perfect pile of wood is just a push away from falling on a patrol of 3 soldiers, making the perfect "accident" to solve your upcoming path. 

No matter your playstyle there's plenty of good fun to be had and liberty on how you decide to approach each scenario.

However despite the bugs that made gameplay frustrating I still enjoyed it enough to finish the campaign as it was not too long a game.

Partisans is a commando-inspired RTS with elements of management of a russian insurgency in german-occupied USSR. What i said above is a good enough taste of what kind of "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!" moment you will experience playing this game. Sadly it is full of them. The game runs like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ turd. No, really, my computer aint too nice or anything but the game looks like ♥♥♥♥ and it cant hit 30 FPS on the main menu. Its seriously strange.

That being said i stil strongly recommend this game, i think its fantastic, i never intended to refund it even when i got frustrated with it and i plan to play it to completition.

Before you decide to buy it or not, however, i believe that if you work on UI or UX design you -HAVE- to play this game
This game is the PERFECT example of how NOT to design an UI. No, graphically its fine, it looks pretty, simple, and its functional, menus aren't hidden, there are nice audio cues for anything you click.

The issue is the "interactive" part. "What weapon is that?" "What ammo is that?" "What's that item?" You think any logical rational human being would just let you hover the mouse above the icon, maybe if they were a bit mean they would make you leave the mouse there for a few seconds before the info menu would pop up. But no, you have to right click every item- No. You dont JUST have to right click on them, that would be too nice, you have to right click on them to open up the popup menu for the item and click on "information" to get even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nametag. If that doesn't sound annoying, similar weapons of different factions like the Kar98k and the Mosin nagant have an almost identical symbol (no, not identical, but close enough to mistake them) some bullet symbols for different calibers are the very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ same, and having to click on "information" all the time just to see  WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ did you just pick up gets annoying quickly.

The game is FULL of weird awful UX design choices like that that just make the experience an absolute annoyance, even 20 years ago many games knew better than to do some of the things Partisans does. It also has some bugs here and there.

You CANNOT drop items into the ground for some reason. Once you pick them up, if you want them out you MUST destroy this. You can, however, trade itemsbetween characters, but this still presents an issue; you see, characters have 2 weapon slots, and weapons are big and occupy a ton of space. If a character with an empty weapon slot has a full inventory, and another one with 2 weapon slots has the gun in his inventory, you end up in this retarded situation where you would love to re-organize the inventory of both characters, but you cant, since you cant drop items and you cant transfer items directly into the weapons slots, only inventory slots, you are screwed out of picking up more items OR you have to destroy them to move the weapon.

My last complaint has to do with the hitbox detection for the mouse, i pity whoever has to click somewhere in a space between objects, or click on a crate next to a door, because you will have to play with the camera a fair bit just to click on what was obviously an open space for the game to recognize what you wanted to do.

Is this the best commando-like game? No, i think that shadow tactics is a frankly better one, but if you still want the part where you ambush a bunch of nazis in a firefight, i dont know any game that does it better, and even with all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that you have to go through sometimes, i still think that the game is a blast.

The game is also not getting updated anymore. If you see the update history the last one was in december 2020... And that was an announcement for an upcoming major fix patch that never came.
